scenes.headline: Comprehensions
scenes.subtitle: Build lists, dicts and sets in a single line
scenes.narration: Comprehensions are a concise, expressive way to build a new collection from existing data in a single line.

scenes.headline: Three flavors
items: List comprehension: [x for x in data]
Dict comprehension: {k: v for k, v in pairs}
Set comprehension: {x for x in data}
scenes.narration: A list comprehension builds an ordered list by looping over a source and transforming each item. A dict comprehension does the same but produces key-value pairs, which is perfect for reshaping records. A set comprehension gathers unique results, automatically dropping any duplicates. And in all three, an optional if clause lets you filter items out as you build the collection.

scenes.headline: A filtered list comprehension
scenes.code:
readings = [22, 15, 30, 18, 25]
high = [r for r in readings if r > 20]
print(high)
scenes.narration: We loop over each reading, and the expression before the for keyword decides what goes into the new list. The if clause at the end keeps only the readings above twenty. In one readable line this does exactly what a for loop with an append would, so high ends up holding just the large values.

scenes.headline: Comprehension versus loop
scenes.narration: A comprehension expresses a simple transform in one line and often runs faster because the work happens in optimized C. A traditional loop with append takes more lines but gives you room to add branching, logging, or multiple steps. The rule of thumb is to use a comprehension when the logic is simple and fall back to a loop the moment it gets complicated.

scenes.headline: How to read a comprehension
scenes.narration: To read a comprehension, start with the output expression that describes each result, then look at the for clause that provides the items. Next check for any if filter that decides which items survive. Reading it in that order makes even a dense comprehension easy to understand.

scenes.text: Use comprehensions for simple transforms and filters, but keep them readable rather than clever.
scenes.narration: The takeaway is that comprehensions shine for simple transforms and filters, so keep them short and readable rather than trying to be clever.
